opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So a lot of the earlier work on AI for science, and even a lot of the early agent work, tended to fall into one of two buckets. On one side you had very specialized models, like a protein structure predictor or a property classifier, that are incredibly powerful but narrow. They answer a question you've already formulated. On the other side, you had general-purpose language model agents that could chat about science, but they often worked as a single assistant answering one prompt at a time, and they didn't really carry a research project from an open-ended question all the way to something you could test at the bench.

With Virtual Lab, the idea was to take inspiration from how real interdisciplinary research actually happens. If I'm working on a hard biomedical problem, I don't go to one person who knows everything. I assemble a team: maybe an immunologist, a computational biologist, a machine learning person, and someone whose job is to be critical and poke holes in the plan. So in Virtual Lab, there's a principal investigator agent that, given a research goal, decides what kinds of expertise are needed and then creates those scientist agents. Then they hold meetings. There are team meetings where everyone discusses the overall direction, and individual meetings where one agent goes deep on a specific task, like writing code or designing a computational pipeline.

A couple of design choices were really important for addressing earlier limitations. One is the scientific critic agent. Language models tend to be agreeable and overconfident, and when you have several of them talking, they can reinforce each other's mistakes. Having a dedicated critic whose role is to push back, ask for justification, and flag weak assumptions made a big difference in output quality. Another is having multiple rounds of discussion, and sometimes running several meetings in parallel and then merging the best ideas, which helps with the variability you get from any single model run.

The third piece, and I think the most important, is grounding. We didn't want the agents to just produce a nice-sounding plan. In our case study on designing nanobodies against new SARS-CoV-2 variants, the agents decided on the approach, which was to start from existing nanobodies and modify them rather than design from scratch, and then they built a pipeline combining tools like ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta. They wrote the code, ran it, and proposed specific nanobody designs. Then we actually went into the wet lab and tested them. A good fraction expressed well, and a couple showed improved binding to the newer variants while keeping binding to the original strain. So the loop was closed with real experimental validation, which a lot of earlier efforts didn't do.

The human role also changes. In Virtual Lab, the human researcher is more like a high-level advisor. We'd provide guidance at key points, but the vast majority of the discussion and the work was done by the agents. In our experiments, the human contribution was a very small fraction of the total words exchanged. So it's less like using a tool and more like collaborating with a team that you occasionally steer.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. The agents still make mistakes, and sometimes they're stuck with tools that are a bit out of date relative to the latest literature. Human judgment is still really important, especially in choosing the problem and evaluating results. But I think Virtual Lab shows that structuring AI agents the way we structure human research teams, with roles, meetings, critique, and real tools, gets you much further toward actually doing science, not just talking about it.

r002.rationale: It says earlier agents could produce discussion or plans but did not carry an open-ended question through to something testable, identifying the gap between proposing and executing research.

r003.rationale: It notes that earlier efforts often lacked real experimental validation and contrasts them with Virtual Lab’s wet-lab testing.

r004.rationale: It explains that the PI agent receives a research goal, chooses needed expertise, and that the agents decide on an approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, a lot of the earlier work on AI agents for science fell into one of two camps. One camp was the fully autonomous "AI scientist" vision, where you'd give the system a prompt and it would go off and generate hypotheses, run experiments, and write a paper end to end. Those were exciting demos, but when you looked closely, the science was often shallow. The agent would produce something that looked like research but didn't really engage with the hard, domain-specific decisions that make a project succeed or fail. And there was no good way for a human expert to steer it.

The other camp was the single assistant model, basically a very capable chatbot that a researcher talks to. That's useful, but it's limited in a different way. A single model is being asked to simultaneously be the immunologist, the computational biologist, the machine learning person, and the skeptical reviewer, and it tends to collapse those perspectives into one bland average. Real science doesn't work that way. The interesting ideas come out of disagreement and specialization.

What we tried to do with Virtual Lab was sit in between those two. The core idea is that you have a principal investigator agent that leads a team of specialized scientist agents, each with their own role and expertise, plus a critic agent whose entire job is to push back and find flaws. They hold structured meetings, team meetings where they debate the overall strategy, and individual meetings where a single agent goes deep on a specific task, like writing code or designing a protocol. And critically, the human researcher is in the loop at the level of setting the agenda and giving feedback, rather than micromanaging every step or being completely cut out.

Two things fall out of that design that I think address the earlier limitations. First, the multi-agent structure gives you genuine diversity of perspective. We saw cases where, say, the computational biologist agent proposed something and the immunologist agent flagged a practical issue with it that the other wouldn't have raised. The critic agent in particular was surprisingly valuable in catching sloppy reasoning. Second, because the human is contributing guidance at the right level of abstraction, you get the benefits of expert judgment without the human having to do all the work. In the nanobody project we did with the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, the human input was something like a few sentences per meeting, and the agents did the heavy lifting of choosing tools like ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta, writing the pipeline, and iterating on designs.

And then the last piece, which I think is really important, is that we actually went and validated the outputs experimentally. The agents designed nanobodies targeting recent SARS-CoV-2 variants, and two of them showed binding in the wet lab. That closes the loop in a way a lot of earlier agent papers didn't. It's one thing to have an agent that produces plausible-sounding science, and another to have one that produces something that works when you test it. I don't think Virtual Lab solves everything, there are plenty of open questions about how far you can push the autonomy and how you keep the agents honest, but I think it points toward a more realistic model of human-AI collaboration in research.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier autonomous agents lacked human steering, but does not say humans prescribed the research steps while agents merely implemented them.

r002.rationale: It describes earlier systems as either autonomous end-to-end agents or single assistants, without identifying a gap between proposing research ideas and executing them.

r003.rationale: It says earlier agent papers often lacked experimental validation and contrasts plausible-sounding science with outputs tested in the wet lab.

r004.rationale: It says the human sets the agenda and gives high-level feedback while agents choose tools, write the pipeline, and iterate on designs.

astra-6.text:
I think one limitation of earlier approaches is that they often focus on a single agent doing a fairly narrow task. But science is rarely like that. If you look at how a research project actually works, you need different kinds of expertise, and you need people to challenge one another’s assumptions. You also need a way to connect those discussions to concrete experiments.

The idea behind Virtual Lab is to organize AI agents more like a research team. You have a principal investigator agent that helps coordinate the project, and specialist agents that contribute different perspectives. They can discuss a question, critique proposed approaches, and work toward a shared research plan, with a human researcher providing direction and feedback.

That structure matters because producing a plausible scientific suggestion is only the beginning. The harder part is making the suggestion specific enough to test, identifying where it might fail, and revising it based on evidence. So the goal is to move from an agent that answers a question toward a team that can help carry a research project through those steps. And ultimately, the measure of success has to be whether the resulting science holds up experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier approaches often use a single agent on a narrow task, but does not say humans prescribe the research steps for agents to implement.

r002.rationale: It describes connecting discussions to experiments and says suggestions need to become testable, but does not clearly identify a proposal-to-execution gap in earlier science agents.

r003.rationale: It says experimental results should determine success, but does not identify limited experimental validation of earlier agents’ research ideas as a weakness.

r004.rationale: The response says agents discuss a question and work toward a shared plan with human direction, but does not clearly state that they determine an approach from a high-level human goal.

sol-6.1.text:
One limitation of earlier approaches is that you often have a single agent trying to do everything. But science involves many different kinds of expertise, and even a very capable scientist needs collaborators who can challenge assumptions and bring different perspectives.

The idea behind Virtual Lab is to create a team of AI scientists with complementary expertise. There’s an AI principal investigator that helps organize the research, and specialist agents that work together through meetings. A human researcher sets the direction and can provide feedback, but doesn’t have to specify every step.

What’s useful about that structure is that the agents can critique each other’s proposals and refine a plan before carrying it out. Of course, agreement among AI agents doesn’t establish that something is scientifically correct. You still need experiments. So I see Virtual Lab as a way to connect that collaborative reasoning process to concrete, testable research, with human scientists guiding the work and experimental results providing the feedback.

r002.rationale: It describes refining a plan before carrying it out, but does not identify a gap between proposing ideas and execution in earlier agents.

r003.rationale: It says experiments are needed to establish correctness, but does not describe limited experimental validation as a weakness of earlier agents’ ideas.

r004.rationale: The human sets the research direction without specifying every step, while the agents critique proposals and refine a plan, conveying that agents work out an approach from human direction.
